intro.data: ONE join must face TWO requests over the same source: a MATCHING request whose ids line up (3,3) and a MISMATCHED request whose ids clash (3,9). The pullback joins on the key, so it pairs the matching request into a real joined row and REFUSES the mismatched one — returning a no-match marker, never a stranger. Bring the joined-row table and the key-respecting join and projection from the tray, and wire each request through to the customer side. A sneaky 'Force-Join' returns the right customer on the matching request but fabricates a pair for the mismatched one, so it passes the easy case and fails the hard one. A join that only handles the matching request is still wrong; build the one that nails BOTH. Leave the loose join and mis-projection in the tray.
intro.alchemy: ONE pairing must face TWO ores over the same source: a MATCHING ore whose marks line up (3,3) and a MISMATCHED ore whose marks clash (3,9). The pullback pairs on the mark, so it matches the lined-up ore into a real pair and REFUSES the clashing one — yielding a no-match marker, never a wrong reagent. Bring the matched-pair vessel and the mark-respecting match and projection from the tray, and wire each ore through to the reagent side. A sly 'Force-Match' yields the right reagent on the matching ore but fabricates a pair for the clashing one, passing the easy case and failing the hard one. A pairing that only handles the matching ore is still false; build the one that nails BOTH. Leave the loose match and mis-projection in the tray.
intro.spellcraft: ONE bind must face TWO runes over the same source: a MATCHING rune whose sigils line up (3,3) and a MISMATCHED rune whose sigils clash (3,9). The pullback binds on the sigil, so it pairs the lined-up rune into a real pair and REFUSES the clashing one — yielding a no-match marker, never a wrong ward. Bring the matched-pair flame and the sigil-respecting bind and projection from the tray, and wire each rune through to the ward side. A sly 'Force-Bind' yields the right ward on the matching rune but fabricates a pair for the clashing one, passing the easy case and failing the hard one. A bind that only handles the matching rune is still hollow; build the one that nails BOTH. Leave the loose bind and mis-projection in the tray.
intro.abstract: Here a pair (a,b) is the carried value and a prime b′ is a different value of the same type. Given f : A → C and g : B → C, the pullback A×_C B holds only the matching pairs (a,b) with f(a)=g(b); the unique mediating map u : X → A×_C B builds that pair from a request and otherwise yields the no-match marker ⊥. Over the same X two cases run: a consistent request (3,3) with f(a)=g(b) must reach 3, and an inconsistent request (3,9) with f(a)≠g(b) must reach ⊥. From the tray bring A×_C B, the key-respecting u, and the projection p₂, and wire X → A×_C B → B for BOTH cases; an impostor u? builds (3,3) for the consistent request but force-fits (3,9) for the inconsistent one, so it passes case 1 and fails case 2. Leave the loose map and mis-projection behind.

goal.abstract: Place A×_C B and the faithful u and p₂, and wire one X → A×_C B → B that sends (3,3) ↦ 3 and (3,9) ↦ ⊥.

afterSuccess.data: One join handled both requests: it paired the matching request into a real joined row and returned customer 3, and it REFUSED the mismatched request with a no-match marker rather than inventing a customer. That refusal is the heart of the pullback — it keeps ONLY the pairs whose keys agree (f∘p₁ = g∘p₂). 'Force-Join' returned the right customer on the easy request but fabricated a row for the clashing one, so it passed case 1 and failed case 2. The mismatched request is why a join must respect the key on every input, not just the ones that happen to line up.
afterSuccess.alchemy: One pairing handled both ores: it matched the lined-up ore into a real pair and returned reagent 3, and it REFUSED the clashing ore with a no-match marker rather than inventing a reagent. That refusal is the pullback: only pairs whose marks agree. 'Force-Match' fabricated a pair for the clashing ore, passing the easy case and failing the hard one.
afterSuccess.spellcraft: One bind handled both runes: it paired the lined-up rune into a real pair and returned ward 3, and it REFUSED the clashing rune with a no-match marker rather than inventing a ward. That refusal is the pullback: only pairs whose sigils agree. 'Force-Bind' fabricated a pair for the clashing rune, passing the easy case and failing the hard one.
afterSuccess.abstract: f∘p₁ = g∘p₂ held on both cases: the pullback admits the consistent pair (3,3) and projects to 3, and it sends the inconsistent (3,9) to ⊥ because no matching pair exists. u? coincides with u on the consistent request — both build (3,3) — so it passes case 1, but it force-fits (3,9) instead of ⊥ and projects to 9, failing case 2. Two cases pin the mediating map: agreeing on one input is not the universal property.

reveal.summary: The pullback of f : A → C and g : B → C is the object of matching pairs — those with f(a) = g(b) — with projections p₁, p₂ and the universal property that any request factors through a UNIQUE mediating map. Two test cases over one map force it to respect the key everywhere: the consistent request must reach the matched element, and the inconsistent one must reach the no-match marker, not a fabricated row.
notation: u : X → A ×_C B with p₂ ∘ u
reveal.moreFormal: The no-match marker is the pullback being EMPTY for that request: when no (a,b) has f(a)=g(b), the matching-pair object contributes nothing, so the honest mediating map cannot fabricate an element. Reversing the arrows dualises the pullback to a pushout.
reveal.programmerAnalogy: orders.join(customers).on(o => o.customerId === c.id): a matching key yields the row, a clashing key yields no row — never a stranger. A unit test on a matching input can pass a buggy join; a mismatched input catches it.
